intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant pseudohypoaldosteronism type I (PHA1A) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding the mineralocorticoid receptor (NR3C2; 600983) on chromosome 4q31.23.

checks.claim: Autosomal dominant pseudohypoaldosteronism type I (PHA1A) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding the mineralocorticoid receptor (NR3C2).
checks.evidence_quote: We conclude that hMR mutations are a common feature of autosomal dominant PHA1, being found in 70% of our familial cases.
checks.explanation: Abstract reports heterozygous hMR mutations in autosomal dominant PHA1.

checks.evidence_quote: PCR and direct sequencing of the MR gene identified a heterozygous point mutation
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature added to the MR gene that the paper names. The abstract itself never states the location.

paragraphs.text: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type I (PHA1) is a primary form of mineralocorticoid resistance. In the newborn it presents with renal salt wasting, dehydration, hypotension, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis and failure to thrive, even though plasma aldosterone and plasma renin activity are elevated (Geller et al., 1998; Tajima et al., 2000; Pujo et al., 2007). Compared with the severe, multiorgan autosomal recessive form, which persists into adulthood and is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), the autosomal dominant or sporadic form is milder and improves gradually with age (Geller et al., 1998; Tajima et al., 2000). Inactivating mutations in the mineralocorticoid receptor gene (MR; NR3C2) cause the autosomal dominant form and some sporadic cases (Pujo et al., 2007).

checks.claim: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type I (PHA1) is a primary form of mineralocorticoid resistance.
checks.evidence_quote: Type 1 pseudohypoaldosteronism (PHA1) is a primary form of mineralocorticoid resistance

checks.claim: In the newborn, PHA1 presents with renal salt wasting, dehydration, hypotension, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis and failure to thrive.
checks.evidence_quote: PHA1) is a rare condition characterized by neonatal salt loss with dehydration, hypotension, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis, despite elevated plasma aldosterone levels and PRA.
checks.explanation: The abstract lists salt loss, dehydration, hypotension, hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis. It does not mention failure to thrive and does not specify renal salt wasting.

checks.claim: In PHA1, plasma aldosterone and plasma renin activity are elevated.
checks.evidence_quote: despite elevated plasma aldosterone levels and PRA
checks.explanation: The abstract states that plasma aldosterone and plasma renin activity (PRA) are elevated.

checks.claim: The autosomal recessive form of PHA1 is severe, multiorgan and persists into adulthood.
checks.evidence_quote: An autosomal recessive form manifests severe life-long salt wasting resulting from multiple mineralocorticoid target tissue such as sweat, salivary glands, the colonic epithelium, and lung.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes the recessive form as severe, life-long and involving multiple target tissues.

checks.claim: The autosomal recessive form of PHA1 is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC).
checks.evidence_quote: This form is caused by loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding subunits of the amiloride-sensitive epithelial sodium channel (ENaC; refs 2,3).

checks.claim: The autosomal dominant or sporadic form of PHA1 is milder than the recessive form and improves gradually with age.
checks.evidence_quote: Contrary, an autosomal dominant PHA1 manifests milder salt wasting that gradually improves with advancing age.
checks.explanation: The abstract states that the dominant form is milder and improves with age.

checks.evidence_quote: Inactivating mutations of the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR; NR3C2) are responsible for autosomal dominant and some sporadic cases of PHA1.

paragraphs.text: Armanini et al. (1985) studied 3 patients with pseudohypoaldosteronism from 2 families. One was a 28-year-old index case from Melbourne. The other 2 were sibs from Munich, aged 8 and 2 years, whose parents were first cousins. The younger sib, a boy, was less severely affected than his sister. The authors described the syndrome as salt wasting and failure to thrive, usually presenting in infancy with high urinary sodium despite hyponatremia, together with hyperkalemia, hyperreninemia and elevated aldosterone levels.

paragraphs.text: Hanukoglu (1991) described a kindred (kindred I) with renal type I pseudohypoaldosteronism. The propositus presented in infancy with renal salt wasting, including vomiting, failure to thrive, short stature, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. He responded dramatically to a high-salt diet (2.5 g/day), and sodium supplementation was stopped at age 2 years. In 7 additional family members from 3 generations, clinical expression ranged from asymptomatic to moderate.

paragraphs.text: Armanini et al. (1985) found that Percoll-separated monocytes from controls bound [3H]aldosterone with high affinity (Kd about 3 nM) and limited capacity (150 to 600 sites per cell). On repeated testing, monocytes from 2 of their 3 patients showed no [3H]aldosterone binding. The third, less severely affected patient had 62 sites per cell, more than 2 SD below the control level. The parents of the Munich sibs had normal levels. The authors concluded that pseudohypoaldosteronism is caused by a defect, complete or partial, in the type I (mineralocorticoid) receptor.

paragraphs.text: Hanukoglu (1991) described a second kindred in which the propositus, the child of a consanguineous marriage, developed severe renal salt losing at age 9 days. She also had increased salivary and sweat electrolytes, which indicated unresponsiveness to mineralocorticoids in multiple target organs. Life-threatening salt wasting recurred after age 2, and at 5 years she needed 14 g/day of salt. A sister died at 9 days with PHA symptoms, and the pedigree was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. From these kindreds and the literature, the author concluded that type I PHA comprises 2 clinically and genetically distinct entities, one with renal defects and one with defects in multiple target organs.

paragraphs.text: Geller et al. (1998) screened the mineralocorticoid receptor gene in 13 dominant or sporadic PHA1 kindreds. They found heterozygous mutations in 1 sporadic and 4 dominant kindreds: 2 frameshift mutations (1 of them de novo), 2 premature termination codons and 1 splice donor mutation. paragraphs.text: Sartorato et al. (2003) analyzed the mineralocorticoid receptor gene in 14 families with autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1 and found 6 different heterozygous mutations. Three of them, 2 frameshifts and 1 nonsense mutation, were predicted to produce truncated proteins. The other 3 were missense mutations, which were studied functionally. paragraphs.text: Riepe et al. (2006) identified 6 different heterozygous NR3C2 mutations in 6 patients with PHA1: a previously reported frameshift mutation (c.1131dupT), a second frameshift (c.2871dupC), 2 novel nonsense mutations generating a truncated receptor protein, and 2 missense mutations (S818L and E972G). Functional and structural studies showed that the c.2871dupC, S818L and E972G mutants lost or had markedly reduced aldosterone binding and transactivation. The authors concluded that their data extended the spectrum of PHA1-causing NR3C2 mutations.

paragraphs.text: Pujo et al. (2007) carried out a comprehensive screen of the NR3C2 gene in patients with PHA1. They searched coding regions, intron-exon junctions and untranslated exons for nucleotide substitutions, and also looked for large deletions. They found 22 MR gene abnormalities in 33 patients. The authors concluded that MR mutations are extremely frequent in PHA1 patients classified according to aldosterone and potassium levels.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a Japanese family with a renal form of PHA1A, Tajima et al. (2000) used PCR and direct sequencing to identify a heterozygous mutation in the NR3C2 gene. The mutation changed codon 924 from CTG to CCG, resulting in a leu924-to-pro (L924P) substitution. In COS-1 cells transfected with a GRE-tk-CAT reporter, aldosterone increased CAT activity with wildtype receptor but had no effect with the L924P mutant. The authors attributed the mineralocorticoid resistance in this family to the mutation.

checks.evidence_quote: We studied the molecular mechanisms of one Japanese family with a renal form of PHA1.

checks.claim: Tajima et al. (2000) used PCR and direct sequencing to identify a heterozygous NR3C2 mutation in affected members of a Japanese family with renal PHA1A.
checks.evidence_quote: PCR and direct sequencing of the MR gene identified a heterozygous point mutation changing codon 924 Leu (CTG) to CCG (Pro) (L924P) in all affected members.
checks.explanation: The abstract gives the method and the heterozygous mutation in affected members.

checks.claim: The NR3C2 mutation in the Japanese PHA1A family changed codon 924 from CTG to CCG, resulting in a leu924-to-pro (L924P) substitution.

checks.explanation: The codon change (CTG to CCG) and the L924P substitution match the abstract exactly.

checks.evidence_quote: Aldosterone increased CAT activity in cells expressing wild-type receptor, but had no effect in cells expressing the mutant receptors.

checks.evidence_quote: These results suggest that mineralocorticoid resistance in this family is due to a missense mutation in the MR gene.

paragraphs.text: In a patient with sporadic PHA I, Viemann et al. (2001) identified a frameshift mutation, an insertion of C at position 2871 (ins2871C), in exon 9 of the mineralocorticoid receptor gene. The mutation was not found in the patient's asymptomatic family members. It was the first mutation described in exon 9 and affects the last 27 amino acids of the hormone-binding domain.

checks.evidence_quote: In the sporadic case we identified a new frameshift mutation, Ins2871C, in exon 9 of the hMR gene.
checks.explanation: "Insertion of C at position 2871" spells out the paper's notation Ins2871C.

checks.claim: The ins2871C mineralocorticoid receptor mutation was not found in the asymptomatic family members of the sporadic PHA I patient.
checks.evidence_quote: Family members were asymptomatic and had no mutation.

checks.claim: The ins2871C mutation was the first mineralocorticoid receptor mutation described in exon 9.
checks.evidence_quote: This mutation is the first described in exon 9 and impairs the last 27 amino acids of the hormone-binding domain.

checks.claim: The ins2871C mineralocorticoid receptor mutation affects the last 27 amino acids of the hormone-binding domain.
checks.evidence_quote: This mutation is the first described in exon 9 and impairs the last 27 amino acids of the hormone-binding domain.
checks.explanation: The draft says "affects" where the paper says "impairs"; the meaning is the same.
